frase_gancho.texto: A clay woman painted with diamond patterns, saved from the waters of a dam.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the surface we go down into the depths. Look for a reconstructed tomb: a vertical shaft leading to an underground chamber surrounded by clay figures.

guion_corto.texto: This clay female figure, almost fifty centimeters tall, comes from Chupícuaro, in Guanajuato, and was made between 400 BC and 200 AD. She has a rounded belly, broad hips, and her hands resting on her belly. Look closely at the paint: red, black, and cream, with diamond patterns on the legs, zigzag bands on the forehead, and geometric masks around the eyes. The surface is polished and shiny. Figures like this were placed in tombs and perhaps on family altars, and they are linked to fertility, motherhood, and the planting of maize. It is one of the most recognizable pieces from the West, and also one of the best painted.

guion_largo.texto:
Today, the place where these figures were found lies underwater. Chupícuaro, in the Lerma River valley, was covered by the Solís Dam more than seventy years ago. But before the water rose, a team of archaeologists arrived in a rush to rescue whatever they could.

They excavated hundreds of burials, surrounded by vessels and figurines, in a race against the water level. Thanks to that rescue we know the Chupícuaro culture today, which would otherwise have been lost forever. It is a reminder that not everything lost from the past is lost through the passing of time: sometimes it is because of a modern construction project.

Their pottery is among the most beautiful in ancient Mexico. Vessels and figures were polished until they shone and were painted in red, black, and cream, with precise geometric designs. Their style is recognizable at first glance, and it resembles pieces found in the Basin of Mexico.

These female figures, with their full forms, pronounced bellies, and broad hips, will remind you of the “[Pretty Ladies](mna_s03_mujeres_bonitas)” of Tlatilco, in the hall of the first villages. It is the same idea: woman as a symbol of fertility, of the maize that sprouts, and of the earth that gives life. But here the paint tells a different story.

The geometric designs covering the body could have been body paint, tattoos, or an imitation of textiles and clothing. As with the [Adolescent of Tamuín](mna_s08_adolescente_huasteco), the body is a page. In many societies, designs on the skin or on clothing told others which group you belonged to, how old you were, or what role you played. If we could read this code, we would know much more about the woman she represents.

Chupícuaro lies at a crossroads. It sits in the Bajío, between the West and the Highlands, on the banks of a river, the Lerma, which connected several valleys. People, goods, and ideas moved through there, and that explains why its style sometimes resembles that of distant regions.

Look at the head: it is broad and flat at the crown. Some Chupícuaro figures show cranial modification, the same custom you saw in the introduction hall and in the profile of [Pakal](mna_s09_mascara_pakal). It was a way of shaping the body from childhood so that it would show belonging and beauty.

And one technical detail: these figures are hollow inside. A solid piece of clay can burst in the kiln, because trapped air expands with heat. That is why potters made hollow pieces with small openings. Besides saving material, this makes them lighter, and it allowed them to be made larger.

And look at the three colors: red, black, and cream. With just three tones, the painters of Chupícuaro achieved designs of almost mathematical precision.

So the next time you see a clay figure more than two thousand years old, remember this story: some pieces reach us by chance, and others, like this one, because someone hurried to save them.

texto: Look for the painted diamonds, zigzags, and geometric masks
Observe the rounded belly and the hands resting on it
Compare its shape with the “Pretty Ladies” of Tlatilco

texto.Material: Polychrome clay (ceramic) in red, black, and white on a light background; modeling, applied clay pellets, and incision

texto.pregunta: Myth: Archaeological sites always remain intact underground.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Some are lost to modern construction. Chupícuaro ended up beneath a dam, and only what was rescued in time was saved.
